questions.text: What is the CORRECT formula for calculating risk?

options.text: Risk = Hazard × Exposure
Risk = Likelihood × Consequence
Risk = Frequency × Duration
Risk = Probability × Population

questions.explanation: Risk = Likelihood (probability of harm occurring) × Consequence (severity of harm if it does occur). This fundamental formula is the basis for all risk matrices used in H&S risk assessment.

questions.text: A risk assessment has been completed for manual handling tasks in a warehouse. Three months later, a new and heavier product line is introduced. What action should be taken?

options.text: No action — the existing risk assessment covers all manual handling
The risk assessment should be reviewed and updated to reflect the changed conditions
A new risk assessment is only needed if there is an accident
Workers should be informed verbally but no documentation is needed

questions.explanation: Risk assessments must be reviewed and updated when there is a significant change in the workplace — including new equipment, substances, processes, or working arrangements. Introducing heavier products changes the manual handling risk profile and requires review.

questions.text: In the hierarchy of controls, which measure is MOST effective at protecting workers?

options.text: Providing appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE)
Introducing administrative controls such as safe working procedures
Eliminating the hazard completely
Improving training and supervision

questions.explanation: Elimination — removing the hazard entirely — is always the most effective control because it removes all possibility of the hazard causing harm. PPE is at the bottom of the hierarchy because it relies on the worker wearing it correctly at all times and does not remove the hazard.

questions.text: A worker repeatedly takes a shortcut through a safe working procedure because it saves time and they have never been hurt doing so. This type of human error is classified as a:

options.text: Slip
Lapse
Mistake
Violation

questions.explanation: A violation is a deliberate deviation from a rule or procedure. The worker knows the correct procedure but chooses not to follow it. Slips and lapses are unintentional attention and memory failures; mistakes involve wrong judgements about the situation.

questions.text: A HAZOP (Hazard and Operability Study) is MOST suitable for:

options.text: Identifying hazards during routine inspection of an office
Examining deviations from design intent in process plant systems
Assessing ergonomic risks at computer workstations
Conducting post-accident investigations

questions.explanation: HAZOP is a formal, structured technique used to identify hazards and operability problems in process plant systems by systematically examining deviations from design intent using guide words (such as 'more than', 'less than', 'reverse'). It is most commonly used in chemical plants, refineries, and process industries.

questions.text: According to the Swiss Cheese Model of accident causation, accidents occur when:

options.text: A single worker makes a critical error
Holes in multiple layers of defence align to allow an accident trajectory to pass through
Safety equipment fails due to poor maintenance
Management fails to conduct regular risk assessments

questions.explanation: James Reason's Swiss Cheese Model illustrates that organisations have multiple layers of defence (like slices of Swiss cheese). Each layer has weaknesses ('holes'). When the holes in all layers align simultaneously, the accident trajectory passes through and an accident occurs. No single failure causes an accident — it requires multiple system failures.

questions.text: What is the MAIN purpose of a Permit to Work (PTW) system?

options.text: To provide a permanent record for insurance purposes
To formally authorise high-risk work with defined controls verified before work starts
To replace the need for a risk assessment
To satisfy government regulatory requirements only

questions.explanation: A Permit to Work system formally authorises specific people to carry out specific high-risk work in a specific location at a specific time, with defined control measures verified before work commences. It is a communication and control document, not a substitute for risk assessment.

questions.text: An individual factor that can increase the likelihood of human error is:

options.text: Strong organisational safety culture
Fatigue due to excessive working hours or shift work
Use of well-designed, ergonomically optimised tools
Clear, simple written procedures with diagrams

questions.explanation: Fatigue is a significant individual factor that impairs attention, decision-making, reaction time, and memory — all of which increase the probability of slips, lapses, and mistakes. It is particularly important in shift work industries such as O&G, healthcare, and construction.

questions.text: When evaluating risk, which combination produces the highest risk score?

options.text: Likelihood 2, Severity 5 (Risk = 10)
Likelihood 3, Severity 4 (Risk = 12)
Likelihood 5, Severity 4 (Risk = 20)
Likelihood 4, Severity 4 (Risk = 16)

questions.explanation: Risk = Likelihood × Severity. L5 × S4 = 20 is the highest score among these options. In a standard 5×5 risk matrix, scores of 20–25 are typically in the 'critical' or 'intolerable' zone requiring immediate action.

questions.text: A Task Risk Assessment (TRA) is conducted before work on a Gulf O&G project. The main advantage of involving workers in the TRA process is:

options.text: It reduces the legal liability of the HSE department
Workers have practical knowledge of task hazards that managers may not be aware of
It means workers cannot claim they were not consulted
It speeds up the assessment process

questions.explanation: Workers performing a task have first-hand knowledge of the practical hazards, difficulties, and shortcuts involved. Their participation in risk assessment is valuable not just legally but practically — it produces better, more relevant assessments and increases worker ownership of safety controls.

questions.text: Substitution in the hierarchy of controls means:

options.text: Replacing one worker with a more experienced one
Replacing a hazardous substance or process with one that presents less risk
Using PPE instead of engineering controls
Sub-contracting hazardous work to another company

questions.explanation: Substitution means replacing something hazardous with something less hazardous. Examples: replacing a solvent-based paint with water-based; replacing a toxic chemical with a less toxic alternative; replacing manual handling with mechanical handling. The hazard is reduced, not eliminated.

questions.text: ALARP means that risk has been reduced to a level where:

options.text: There is zero risk of harm to any worker
All possible controls have been applied regardless of cost
Further risk reduction would require effort grossly disproportionate to the benefit gained
Risk has been reduced below the legal minimum

questions.explanation: ALARP (As Low As Reasonably Practicable) means reducing risk until the cost (time, money, effort) of further reduction would be grossly disproportionate to the safety benefit. It is not zero risk — zero risk is rarely achievable. It is the legal standard used in UK, Australia, and referenced by international standards.
